generals.title: The Generals' Letter
generals.author: Ines Varga
pages: Picture a ring of generals camped round a city. They can only talk by messenger, and they must all attack together or all hold back. A half-hearted attack is the worst outcome of all.
Now suppose some generals are traitors. A traitor can tell one neighbour “attack” and another “retreat”. Messengers can be late. Nobody can see into anyone else's tent.
Computer scientists call this the Byzantine Generals Problem. A system that still agrees when some members lie, go silent or tell different peers different things is called Byzantine fault tolerant.
A federation of guardians is such a system. The honest guardians do not need to know who the traitors are. They need enough honest voices, and a rule that turns those voices into one decision.

third.title: One in Three
third.author: Tomas Oyelaran
pages: How many liars can a group survive? For agreement that never splits, fewer than a third. A federation of n guardians can tolerate f faulty ones only when n is greater than 3f.
Why a third? Any two groups big enough to decide must share at least one honest member. If more than a third could lie, two opposite decisions could both look valid, and the federation would split.
So four guardians survive one bad one, seven survive two, and ten survive three. A fifth or sixth guardian buys no extra safety; only the seventh makes a second failure safe.
Remember the arithmetic at a council vote. Every honest guardian rotated out by mistake brings the Byzantines closer to that third, and once they reach it the federation stops.

blind.title: Blind Ink
blind.author: Mara Quell
pages: A mint signs a note so everyone knows it is real. But if the mint sees every note it signs, it can follow each one from the person who asked for it to the person who spends it.
A blind signature fixes this. You seal your note inside a blinding envelope before you hand it over, and the mint signs through the envelope without seeing what is inside.

Back home you take the envelope off. The signature still holds on the note underneath, yet the mint has never seen it. When the note comes back to be spent, the mint can check the signature but cannot tell whose note it was.
David Chaum described this idea in 1982, and it is the heart of ecash. In a federation the guardians run the mint together, so no single guardian can sign notes alone or quietly print more.

twice.title: Spent Twice
twice.author: Kofi Adeyemi
pages: A paper note cannot sit in two pockets at once. A digital note is only a number, and numbers can be copied. So what stops someone spending the same note twice?
The mint keeps a list of every note already spent. When a note comes in, the guardians check the list. If the note is on it, it is refused; if not, it is accepted and added.
The guardians must agree on that list. If one guardian took a note that another refused, the same coin could be spent in two places. That is why every spend goes through consensus.
In the Ledger Archive you hunt for exactly this: a note that turns up twice, or a signature that does not match. Catching one keeps the whole federation honest.

powers.title: Notes of Two
powers.author: Lucia Brandt
pages: Ecash notes come in fixed sizes: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and on, each double the last. Any amount can be made from them, the way any number can be written in binary.
Fixed sizes help privacy. When everyone's notes come in the same few amounts, a note of 64 sats says nothing about who holds it or what it was for.
When you pay, you hand over notes that cover the price. The mint takes them in and issues fresh notes for your change, so nothing you spent can be linked to what you get back.

That is why the shops of Beach Town and Port Concord ask you to pick notes from your wallet. Handing over a note you do not need is refused: the mint makes change, but it will not take more than you owe.

keepers.title: The Keepers of Port Concord
keepers.author: Abena Mensah
pages: A federated mint is run by a group of guardians instead of one company. Each guardian holds a share of the signing key, and no share can sign anything on its own.
To sign, a threshold of guardians must agree. With four guardians the threshold is three; with seven it is five. Below the threshold, nothing moves.

Guardians are usually people who already trust each other: a town's shopkeepers, a community's elders, friends who keep servers running. The federation spreads trust out instead of piling it in one place.
Being a guardian is a duty, not a crown. You keep your server up, check every proposal, and refuse to sign what you cannot verify. That is the whole job, and the whole game.

harbourTales.title: Harbour Tales: Stories of Port Concord Folk
harbourTales.author: Wren Osei
pages: The Umbrella Lender. Every wet Tuesday, Mrs Dorothea Pike of the Saltmarket fish hall props a bucket of umbrellas beside her stall under a sign: BORROW ONE, BRING ONE. In thirty years she has never bought an umbrella. The bucket simply refills, with black ones, striped ones and one shaped like a duck. Last spring a sailor returned an umbrella he had borrowed as a boy. “Sorry it's late,” he said. “I've been round the Cape twice.” She gave him a herring for his honesty.

The Baker of Low Tide. The streets of Low Tide are rough, but at four each morning they smell of cardamom. That is Ravi Menon's bakery, which has no sign because it needs none. Each night Ravi leaves a tray of the day's leftover buns on the step for whoever needs one. Once, somebody took the whole tray. The next night it came back, scrubbed, with a thank-you note and a loaf of their own, slightly burnt. Ravi pinned the note above the oven, where it still hangs, browning gently.

Night Shift on Signet Row. Nurse Imogen Tal has worked nights at the hospital for eleven years, and for nine of them a pigeon has tapped at her window at three o'clock sharp. She calls him the Registrar, because he inspects everything and approves of nothing. One winter the Registrar stopped coming, and Imogen was surprised how much she minded. In March he returned with a mate and a twig, and built a nest on the ledge, right beside the sign that says NO NESTING.

The Gull Counter. On the rocks of Gullmoor sits Barnaby Quist with a notebook and a pencil stub, counting gulls. He has counted them every morning since he retired from the ferries, though nobody ever asked him to. “Somebody ought to know,” he says. The number is usually about four hundred. Once it was four hundred and one, and Barnaby spent a whole week finding out why. It was a tern: lost, embarrassed and, in his considered opinion, very welcome.

gullSongs.title: Gull Songs and Other Harbour Verses
gullSongs.author: Hettie Gorse, Poet of Gullmoor
pages: Gull on the Bollard. Gull on the bollard, gull on the mast, / gull on the fishmonger's awning at last; / gull with a chip and a terrible plan, / gull who has pinched the whole lunch of a man. / Gull at the Mint Hall, inspecting the queue, / eyeing the notes as a guardian would do; / squinting, suspicious, he cocks up his head: / “Is that a real one? Or is it just bread?”

Low Tide. The water goes out like a guest who's been told / the party is over, the soup's getting cold. / It leaves on the mudflats its spoons and its keys, / a boot and a bottle, a crab and some peas. / Then back it comes, sheepish, at twenty past ten, / and tucks in the harbour like nothing has been, / and the boats that were lying askew on the sand / sit up and look round as if all had been planned.

Lantern Night. On lantern night the harbour wears / a thousand tiny lights; / they bob along like whispered prayers / and fish look up in fright. / The boats all nod, the gulls go still, / the ferry dims its beam, / and every window on the hill / leans out to watch the stream. / And somewhere past the Shallows' edge / the last small lantern sails, / to tell the moon the town has pledged / to keep its promises and tales.

The Ferryman's Lullaby. Hush now, the tide is turning, / the buoys are ringing slow; / the Concord light is burning / to guide the boats below. / The nets are dry and folded, / the gulls have gone to bed, / the moon, a coin of silver, / is rolling overhead. / So close your eyes, my sailor, / the harbour keeps its watch, / and morning, like a tailor, / will stitch the sky with gold.

saltKitchen.title: The Salt Kitchen: Recipes from the Harbour
saltKitchen.author: Auntie Priya Fernandes of Saltmarket
pages: Saltmarket Fishcakes (makes 8). Boil 500 g floury potatoes until soft, then drain and mash. Poach 400 g white fish or smoked haddock in milk for 6 minutes, then flake it, minding the bones. Mix fish and mash with a handful of chopped parsley, a spoon of capers, lemon zest, salt and pepper. Shape into eight patties and chill for 30 minutes. Dip each in flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs. Fry in a little oil, 3 to 4 minutes a side, until golden. Serve with lemon wedges and peas.

Low Tide Chowder (serves 4). Fry 4 rashers of chopped bacon in a big pot until crisp. Add a diced onion and two sticks of celery and soften for 5 minutes. Stir in a spoon of flour, then 500 ml fish or vegetable stock and 2 diced potatoes. Simmer 12 minutes, until the potatoes are tender. Add 400 g white fish in chunks and a handful of sweetcorn, and simmer 5 minutes more. Pour in 250 ml milk or cream, warm it through without boiling, and season with pepper and thyme.

Mint Hall Masala Chai (serves 2). In a small pan, bring 250 ml water to the boil with 4 crushed green cardamom pods, a thumb of grated ginger, 2 cloves and a small piece of cinnamon. Simmer 3 minutes. Add 2 teaspoons of loose black tea, such as Assam, and simmer 1 minute more. Pour in 250 ml milk and bring it back to a gentle boil, watching closely: chai rises fast and loves to escape. Sweeten to taste, strain into cups, and drink while arguing about the tide tables.

Tidewater Temple Dal (serves 4). Rinse 200 g red lentils until the water runs clear. Simmer them in 800 ml water with half a teaspoon of turmeric for 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until soft and creamy, then add salt. In a small pan, heat 2 tablespoons of ghee or oil, add a teaspoon of cumin seeds and let them sizzle. Add a chopped onion, 2 cloves of garlic, a little ginger and a green chilli, and fry until golden. Tip this tarka into the dal, squeeze in lemon, scatter coriander and serve with rice.

A Word from the Kitchen. Fresh fish smells of the sea, not of the fish hall floor; if in doubt, ask the fishmonger, and if the fishmonger looks away, buy the lentils. Wash your hands after handling raw fish, cook it until it turns opaque and flakes easily, and keep little hands well away from hot oil. Every recipe in this book was tested on the guardians of the Mint, who are fussy, and on the gulls of Gullmoor, who are not.

lighthouseKid.title: Pip and the Concord Light
lighthouseKid.author: Marigold Tenpenny
pages: At the very tip of Gullmoor, past the last bench and the last bin, stands the Concord Point lighthouse, and in the cottage at its foot lived a girl called Pip. Pip's grandmother kept the light. Every evening she climbed one hundred and twelve steps, wound the great clock that turned the lamp, and polished the glass until it shone like a soap bubble. Pip counted the steps out loud. She was never once wrong, though she sometimes counted the cat.

One stormy night, Grandmother sneezed so hard that she sat down on the stairs and could not get up again. “My knees,” she said, “have resigned.” The lamp was not yet lit. Out in the rain, the night ferry was coming home, and the rocks off Gullmoor were waiting for it, black and patient. Pip looked up at the one hundred and twelve steps. Then she looked at the cat. The cat looked away. “Fine,” said Pip. “I'll go.”

Pip climbed. At step forty the wind howled. At step eighty the tower swayed, just a little, the way towers do. At step one hundred and twelve she found the big brass key, wound the clock exactly as Grandmother did, ten turns and not one more, and lit the lamp. It woke with a whoomph. Its beam swung out over the water, round and round, saying what lighthouses always say: here are the rocks, there is the harbour, come home this way.

Far out, the ferry captain saw the light, turned the wheel, and slipped safely into Port Concord with every passenger dry and grumbling. Next morning the captain climbed the hill with a tin of biscuits and a cushion for Grandmother's knees. And Pip? Pip got a brass badge that said Assistant Keeper, which she wore every day, even in the bath. The cat got a biscuit, which it did not deserve, but which it ate with great dignity.

nightFerry.title: The Night Ferry Affair
nightFerry.author: Constance Fairweather
pages: Chapter One. The 11:40 from the Reef Docks was the last ferry to the Shallows, and Miss Odessa Crane, retired harbour librarian, took it every Thursday for the quiet. Tonight it was not quiet. The saloon held an accordionist who would not stop, a fishmonger with a cool box, a young guardian clutching a leather case, and the purser, Mr Hobb, who was carrying the Regatta Cup in a velvet bag to the committee on the islets. “Nobody touch it,” he announced. Everybody wanted to.

Chapter Two. Halfway across, the lights flickered and went out. For eleven seconds there was only the creak of the hull and one long, startled note from the accordion. When the lights came back, the velvet bag lay flat on the table. The Cup was gone. Mr Hobb made a sound like a kettle. The captain locked the saloon doors. “Nobody leaves,” she said, “until we're tied up at the Shallows.” Miss Crane put down her cocoa. It was, she felt, going to be one of those Thursdays.

Chapter Three. Miss Crane made a list, because librarians always do. The fishmonger's cool box was very cold and very heavy. The accordionist had wet sleeves, though it was not raining. The young guardian refused to open the leather case, saying only that it held “federation business”. And the purser had polished the Cup that very morning, so his fingerprints proved nothing. By the porthole she found a single gold sequin and a smear of something that smelled of brass polish and peppermint.

Chapter Four. “Mr Hobb,” said Miss Crane, “who knew the Cup would be aboard tonight?” “Only the committee,” said the purser, “and whoever reads the notice board at the Reef Docks.” So, everybody. Miss Crane sighed and looked out of the porthole. Below it, bobbing on a rope in the ferry's dark wake, was a small orange buoy that had not been there when they left. She smiled for the first time all evening. “Captain,” she said, “might we slow down, just a little?” (To be continued.)

charter.title: The Charter of Port Concord
charter.author: The First Council of Port Concord
pages: Preamble. We, the people of Port Concord, fishers and bakers, clerks and keepers, guardians and gulls (the gulls did not sign, but were present), set down these rules so that the harbour may be fair, the streets safe and the soup hot. Where this Charter is unclear, citizens shall choose the kinder reading. Where it is silent, they shall ask a neighbour. Where it contradicts itself, they shall bring biscuits to Council Hill and sort it out.

Article I: The Council. The city is run by a council of nine, chosen by the citizens every three years. No decision binds the city unless a clear majority agree, and no councillor may vote on a matter that pays them. Meetings are open to all. Any citizen may speak for three minutes, timed by the egg-timer kept for that purpose, which may not be tampered with, shaken or hidden in a hat.

Article II: The Harbour. The harbour belongs to everyone, and no one may block it. Every boat gives way to a boat in distress. The lighthouse at Concord Point shall be lit every night without exception, even on holidays, even in a sulk. Fish sold in Saltmarket must be honestly weighed, and any scale found to be crooked shall be displayed in City Hall with a label explaining what it did.

Article III: The Mint. The city's notes are signed by a federation of guardians, never by one hand alone. No guardian may sign what they have not checked, and any citizen may ask how the Mint keeps its books. Guardians serve the city; the city does not serve the guardians. A guardian who breaks faith shall be voted out by their fellows, and their robe given to someone with better manners.

Article IV: Neighbours. Every citizen may worship as they choose: at the Harbour Chapel, the mandirs, the Tidewater Temple or on a quiet rock in the Shallows. Every home may hang out washing on Mondays. Noise after midnight is permitted only for weddings, festivals and genuine emergencies, and a seagull is not a genuine emergency. Changes to this Charter need two thirds of the council and one cup of tea per councillor.

harbourHistory.title: From Fish Hut to Free Port: A History of Port Concord
harbourHistory.author: Dr Ambrose Kettlewell, City Archivist
pages: In the beginning there was a sandbar, a spring of fresh water and a family of very stubborn fishers who refused to leave either. They built three huts on the beach at what is now Gullmoor and smoked their catch over driftwood fires. Passing boats came for the water and stayed for the smoked mackerel. Within a generation the three huts were thirty, and someone had built a jetty, mostly out of other people's fences.

The town that grew along the sand was called, without much imagination, Beach Town. It was cheerful, muddy and loud, and every sort of trade washed up there: salt, rope, spices and gossip. When the market outgrew the sand, the traders moved inland onto proper streets and roofed the fish hall in slate. The salt merchants had the biggest stalls and the loudest voices, and by the time the maps were redrawn, Beach Town had become Saltmarket.

As trade grew, so did worry. Pirates were few, but tax collectors from up the coast were many. So the townsfolk built a gatehouse on the hill above the harbour, with one road in and one great oak door. Whoever kept the gate kept the peace. Over the years the gatehouse grew a council chamber, then offices, then a clock, and the hill became Council Hill. The old Gate Tower still stands, and its door still sticks in wet weather.

The last great change came with the Mint. Merchants were tired of trusting a single moneylender who kept his ledger under his hat. So the city chose a federation of guardians to sign its notes together, so that no single keeper could cheat and no single failure could stop the city's money. The Mint Hall was built on the old rope-walk. Port Concord has argued about almost everything since, but never about that.

councilMinutes.title: Minutes of the Council, Meeting No. 1,412
councilMinutes.author: Prudence Ogilvy, Clerk to the Council
pages: Present: the Mayor, eight councillors, the clerk, two members of the public and a gull, which entered through the window at 7:04 and was not minuted further. Apologies: Councillor Fenwick (dentist). The meeting opened at 7:00 with a dispute about whether it had opened at 7:00, since the chamber clock runs four minutes fast. It was agreed that the clock is fast, and that nobody would fix it, as it gets meetings started on time.

Item 1: The bench on Harbour Parade. Councillor Brightwater reported that the bench outside the fish hall wobbles. Councillor Dunmore said it had wobbled for twenty years and the public were fond of it. A member of the public said she was not fond of it and had spilled a chowder. After forty minutes of discussion it was resolved to put a folded beer mat under the short leg, and to review the matter in spring.

Item 2: The Regatta. The regatta will go ahead on the second Saturday of summer. Council noted with regret that last year's winning boat was later found to be a bathtub with a sail. The rules have been amended to say that entries must be boats. Councillor Pike asked whether a bathtub that floats is legally a boat. The Mayor said it was late. The question was referred to a sub-committee, which is Councillor Pike.

Item 3: Any Other Business. The Mint reported all guardians present, all notes balanced, and one biscuit tin missing from the signing room. The tin was later found under the Mayor's chair. The Mayor apologised. Councillor Fenwick arrived from the dentist and voted against everything out of habit, then for everything once it was explained. The meeting closed at 9:41. Next meeting: Thursday, same time, same clock.

tideTables.title: The Concord Almanac of Tides and Signals
tideTables.author: Captain Halvard Nkemelu, Harbourmaster (ret.)
pages: On Tides. The sea rises and falls about twice a day, pulled mostly by the Moon and a little by the Sun. High water comes roughly fifty minutes later each day, because the Moon rises later too. When Sun and Moon line up, at new and full moon, the tides run biggest: these are spring tides, nothing to do with the season. At half-moon the range is smallest: neap tides. Always check the table before mooring in the Shallows, or your boat may spend the afternoon on a sandbank, looking foolish.

On Knots, the Speed. A knot is one nautical mile per hour, and a nautical mile is 1,852 metres, about one minute of latitude. Old sailors measured speed by paying out a log on a line knotted at even spaces and counting the knots that ran out in a set time. On Knots, the Rope. Learn three and the Reef Docks will never laugh at you: the bowline makes a loop that will not slip, the clove hitch ties to a post in a hurry, and the reef knot ties the two ends of one line, as when reefing a sail.

On Signal Flags. Each letter of the alphabet has a flag, and many mean something on their own. Flag A, white and blue, means: I have a diver down, keep well clear at slow speed. Flag B, plain red, means: I am carrying dangerous cargo. Flag O, red and yellow, means: man overboard. Flag P, the Blue Peter, means: all aboard, the ship is about to sail. And the distress signal everyone should know is three short, three long, three short: SOS, by lamp, by horn or by banging on a pot.

On the Right of Way. When two power boats meet head on, both turn to starboard and pass port to port. When two cross, the boat that sees the other on its own starboard side gives way. An overtaking boat always keeps clear of the one it passes. Power generally gives way to sail, and everyone gives way to a vessel that cannot easily steer, such as one fishing with nets. Port is left, with a red light; starboard is right, with a green one. Port and left both have four letters, which helps.

ledgerCraft.title: Ledgercraft: A Clerk's Handbook of Honest Books
ledgerCraft.author: Euphemia Rook, Chief Clerk, Council Hill
pages: Every sum has two sides. That is the whole secret of double-entry bookkeeping, worked out by careful merchants centuries ago. When the bakery buys flour for 50 sats, its cash goes down by 50 and its stock goes up by 50. One account is debited, another is credited, and the two always match. If your debits and credits do not add up to the same total, something has gone wrong, and the books are telling you so before anyone else notices.

The Five Families. Every account belongs to one of five families. Assets are what you own: cash, notes, stock, the cart. Liabilities are what you owe, such as the fishmonger's unpaid bill. Equity is what is left over for the owner. Income is money earned, and expenses are money spent to earn it. The great rule that binds them is simple: assets equal liabilities plus equity. Write it inside the cover of your ledger, and check it every Friday.

On Reconciling. Once a month, lay your own records beside an outside one, such as the Mint Hall's statement of your deposits, and tick off every line that appears in both. Whatever is left needs explaining: a payment still on its way, a fee you forgot, a figure you wrote as 81 when it was 18. Never hide the gap under a mystery line called sundries. Find it. A small difference you cannot explain is often the first sign of a large one.

Why Two Signatures Beat One. The clerk who records a payment should not be the clerk who sends it, and any large payment needs two people to sign. This is not because clerks are wicked. It is because everyone makes mistakes, and now and then someone is tempted. A second pair of eyes catches the slip and discourages the temptation. The Mint takes the idea further: no note is signed until a threshold of guardians agree. Same principle, more robes.

Habits of a Good Clerk. Keep every receipt, dated and filed, for as long as the rules require. Write in ink and never rub out: if you err, strike a single line through the wrong figure so it can still be read, and write the right one beside it. Close the books on the same day each month. Lock the cash box, and keep the key and the box apart. And when someone says the numbers are probably fine, check them anyway. Probably is not a total.

merchantLetters.title: Letters Regarding a Late Cargo
merchantLetters.author: Collected by Hector Lumley, Harbour Archive
pages: Dear Mrs Vance, I write regarding forty crates of cardamom, promised to my shop in Saltmarket by the first of the month. It is now the nineteenth. My chai customers are restless. One has threatened to drink coffee. I paid half in advance, in good Mint notes, as you will recall, and I should like either my cardamom or a very convincing explanation. Yours, with diminishing patience, Bartholomew Crisp, Spices & Sundries.

Dear Mr Crisp, your cardamom is perfectly safe. It is aboard the Gannet, which is becalmed off the southern capes with no wind at all. I cannot order the wind; I have tried. The captain reports that the crew are well and the hold smells wonderful. The crates will be at the Reef Docks the moment the sea allows. In the meantime, might your customers try ginger? Yours, serenely, Ottilie Vance, Vance & Daughters Shipping.

Dear Mrs Vance, ginger! I have sold ginger to these people for eleven years. They know what ginger is. I now hear from the harbourmaster that the Gannet was sighted off Gullmoor last Tuesday, sailing briskly in the opposite direction. Becalmed, madam? Briskly? I enclose the harbourmaster's note. Please explain this, if you can, in words of one syllable. Yours, crossly, B. Crisp.

Dear Mr Crisp, the Gannet was sailing the other way because a fishing boat had lost its nets and its rudder, and my captain towed it home, as every ship must. The crew of the Marlinspike send their thanks, and also a box of smoked mackerel, which I am forwarding to you. The cardamom lands on Thursday. I have knocked a tenth off the balance for your trouble. Yours, a little less serenely, O. Vance.

Dear Mrs Vance, the cardamom has landed, the chai is brewing and the mackerel was excellent. I withdraw the word briskly and every word after it. I paid the balance at the Mint Hall counter less your tenth, then added the tenth back again, because a ship that stops to help another is worth the full price. Next season I should like eighty crates. Please send them on a ship with a little less conscience and a little more wind. Yours, warmly, Bartholomew.
